entries.why: The Act's scope is prose, not a table. Auto-rewriting which situations are protected from a scraped page would let the site's most consequential sentences change without a person reading them.
The shard is a transcription of statutory text. A statute changes by amendment, rarely and deliberately, and the change must be read rather than parsed.
Eleven clocks across four titles of the CFR, each cited to its own section. A missed enrollment window costs a household its coverage, so a human reads every change.
Channel availability and eligibility change by program announcement, not on a schedule — and an absence (Direct File in 2026) is itself a recorded fact.
The ordering framing and consequence language come from the CFPB's own tool. A change there is a reason to re-read the ordering, not to rewrite it automatically.
The qualifying events that open a special enrollment period. The sequence ordering is editorial; this watches the list it is grounded in.

Delaware's standard deduction is statutory and does not index: 30 Del. C. §1108 has set it at $3,250 / $6,500 for every taxable period beginning after December 31, 1999. There is no annual figure to parse, and the section states the amounts as a history of periods without ever using a filing-status label a parser knows — it says "resident spouses ... if they file a joint return". A value adapter is the wrong instrument; a change here is an amendment, and an amendment must be read.

This shard's consequential content is not its threshold — 138% has been the effective ACA figure since 2014 — but the MAP: which of the 51 jurisdictions expanded, since NFIB v. Sebelius made it optional and a state can change position by ballot measure or legislation. The adapter watches the threshold and refuses, so the map was watched by nothing at all, behind a citation note promising a refresh watch covered it. This is the only Medicaid.gov page that states the map in readable text, one row per state with an 'Expansion to Adults' column reading a percentage or 'No' — but it is dated ('based on state decisions as of December 1, 2023'), so parsing it would confirm a 2026 shard forever and could never report a change, the Rev. Proc. 2023-34 trap. Fingerprinting it is the honest half: CMS republishing the table is what a state changing position looks like here, and a person reads the diff. The map was verified row by row against this page on 2026-08-30 and agrees for all 51.

The $25,000 / $32,000 provisional-income thresholds are statutory and were deliberately never indexed — they have not moved since 1983 and 1993, which is why an ever-growing share of benefits is taxable. There is no annual figure for an adapter to chase, so this is Delaware's shape: a change is an amendment somebody reads. Watched at the statute rather than at Pub 915, which is reissued annually at a stable URL and would fire every year about a rule that had not moved.

The AOTC and Lifetime Learning phase-out ranges do not index: § 25A(i) fixed them at $80,000-$90,000 single and $160,000-$180,000 joint, and the 2020 Act aligned the Lifetime Learning range to the same figures rather than continuing to adjust it. The inflation-adjustment procedure states neither, so there is nothing annual to parse and a change is an act of Congress. This list first recorded the opposite, that the ranges index; the statute is watched now partly so that claim stops being taken on trust.

The Uniform Lifetime Table is a regulation, not an indexed figure. Treasury last reissued it effective 2022, on revised mortality assumptions, and it moves only when they are revised again — a rulemaking, which is exactly the kind of change that must be read rather than parsed. Watched at the regulation that contains the table rather than at Pub 590-B, which restates it and is reissued every year.

The full-retirement-age schedule is statutory (42 U.S.C. 416(l)) and keyed to year of birth, so it does not index and has not moved since the 1983 amendments — Delaware's shape again, where a change is an amendment somebody reads. The figures that DO move annually, the wage base and the COLA, live in fica-2024 and the SSA adapter watches those; this shard holds only the part that does not move, which is exactly why nothing was watching it.

The SALT limitation is statutory, not indexed, and it is on a written schedule: IRC §164(b)(7)(A) sets $40,000 for 2025 and $40,400 for 2026, then 101 percent of the prior year through 2029, then back to $10,000. So there is no annual figure for an adapter to chase and every step is a transcription somebody makes deliberately — Delaware's shape, at the statute rather than at a revenue procedure. It is watched at all because the last version of this figure was a constant in the engine with nothing behind it, which is how it stayed at $10,000 for two years after the One Big Beautiful Bill Act replaced it, understating the deduction for anyone itemizing more than $10,000 of state and local tax.
